title: BERISHA & OTHERS v. "THE FORMER YUGOSLAV REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA"
summary:
In Berisha and Others v. "the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia," the applicants—Redjep and Djezide Berisha, along with Djafer, Shanie, and Jashar Berisha—were Yugoslav nationals of Romany origin, falling within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. Their case highlighted the acute vulnerability of Roma families fleeing ethnic violence and facing the threat of expulsion to a region where they risked persecution. In June and July 1999, both families were forced to flee Kosovo after being threatened, attacked, and, in one instance, physically assaulted by armed individuals in KLA uniforms. After entering Macedonia, they were granted temporary humanitarian status but were later arrested for attempting to cross into Bulgaria with forged passports. Following a swift trial, they received suspended sentences and were ordered expelled, raising fears of return to life-threatening conditions.

The applicants complained under Articles 2 and 3 (right to life and prohibition of ill-treatment), Article 13 (right to an effective remedy), and Article 6 (fair trial rights) of the European Convention on Human Rights. However, the European Court of Human Rights found the application inadmissible: the expulsion orders were annulled, and the applicants remained in Macedonia, so they could no longer claim to be victims. The Court also found no arguable claim under Article 13 and noted that the criminal convictions had been quashed, rendering the Article 6 complaints moot.

This case illustrates the precarious situation of Roma and Traveller families displaced by conflict and the procedural hurdles they face in seeking protection. It reflects the broader historical context of Roma vulnerability in post-conflict Europe and the challenges in securing effective remedies through national and international legal systems.
